intro: Sport needs more than players. It needs a body that writes rules, a room to play in and someone who holds the key. In this unit you will meet two kinds of institutions. The first is disability sport: deaf games from 1924, wheelchair basketball from 1949 and the Paralympic movement. The second is the public sport of Illinois: school land, park districts and the Illinois High School Association.

Both stories are about who was let in. Deaf and disabled athletes built their own federations when others left them out. Chicago families fought over who could use a beach or a park. Girls in Illinois waited decades for some state titles. Laws, lawsuits and votes opened many of these doors.

You will be able to name the bodies that run these sports and when they began. You will read laws, reports and records. You will explain how a rule, a tax or a building decided who could play. You will also tell legends apart from records.
bigQuestion: How do public bodies, from federations to park districts, decide who gets to play and where?

test.why: The IHSA dates to 1900; the others came in 1949, 1968 and 1989.

test.q: Who led the international deaf sports committee from its start?
test.why: Deaf leaders founded and ran the committee in 1924.

test.q: What event opened on the same day as the 1948 London Olympics?
test.why: Guttmann held the Stoke Mandeville archery contest on July 29, 1948.

test.q: What Illinois town hosted the first national wheelchair basketball tournament?
test.why: Tim Nugent hosted it in Galesburg in 1949.

test.q: What did the 2001 IOC–IPC agreement set up?
choices: One host city for both Games
test.why: The Olympic host city would also host the Paralympics.

test.q: What does functional classification group athletes by?
choices: What they can do in their sport
test.why: It looks at how an impairment affects a particular sport.

test.q: Which stadium hosted the first International Special Olympics Summer Games?
test.why: They opened at Soldier Field in Chicago in July 1968.

test.q: What does the story of William Hoy and umpire signals show?
choices: A legend can spread without proof
All baseball rules came from Chicago
test.why: Historians find no clear record that Hoy caused umpire signals.

test.q: What did the Land Ordinance of 1785 reserve?
choices: Section 16 of each township for schools
test.why: It set aside section 16 of every township for public schools.

test.q: Why did reformers in the playground movement want city money?
choices: So public play spaces could reach many neighborhoods
test.why: They argued that play space was a public need that governments should fund.

test.q: What did the 1922 report The Negro in Chicago study?
choices: The causes of the 1919 race riot
test.why: The Chicago Commission on Race Relations studied the 1919 riot and its causes.

test.q: Which law of 1990 required access in many public places and businesses?
test.why: The ADA of 1990 covered public places and many private businesses.

test.q: Who votes on changes to IHSA bylaws?
test.why: Proposals reaching the ballot are voted on by member school principals.

test.q: Which statement about park districts in Illinois is true?
choices: They are run by the IHSA
They are separate local governments that can levy taxes
test.why: Illinois park districts are their own units of local government with taxing power.

test.q: What do the IHSA dates 1937 and 2022 show together?
choices: How long girls waited for a wrestling title after boys got one
test.why: Boys wrestling had state finals in 1937; girls wrestling first had them in 2022.

write.prompt: Who decides who gets to play? Choose one disability sport body and one Illinois body from this unit. Cite at least two dated documents or records, such as the 1922 commission report, the 1949 founding of the NWBA, the 2013 letter to schools or IHSA championship records. Explain how each body opened or closed a door.
tips: Name each document or record and give its date.
Say which body made each rule or decision.
Label legends as legends and keep them apart from records.
Compare the two bodies instead of judging only one.
Use unit terms such as governing body, access, eligibility and park district.
